Our planning team has told us that it's going to take three to six months to develop regulations. So until then, we need a pause to ensure that we protect our communities, our residents and our natural resources.

Residents are concerned about the noise, water usage, energy impact and impact on the quality of life. I mean, these are large-scale industrial facilities. In fact, there is one that is being proposed very close to where I live. “Our goal is to be 100 percent carbon-free by 2030. That's our city operational goal,” said at-large council member Dimple Ajmera, who chairs the environment committee.

The proposed council resolution calls on the city to switch entirely to solar and other renewable energy sources, as well as nuclear power by 2030. Nuclear is included, Ajmera said, because the city’s main energy supplier Duke Energy relies heavily on nuclear as part of its energy mix.

Council rep Kimberly Owens challenged someone to show her how the I-77 toll lane project will effectively make life better for the residents of Charlotte. She suggested that council call on the governor to stop the project if the city is unable to do so. “We cannot pave our way to prosperity; let’s look at how we move people, not just how we move cars,” Owens said.

District rep JD Mazuera Arias explained his vote: “We are saturated with gas stations in District 5 and I think we need more amenities and more third spaces for community to gather. As we’ve approved a sales tax to fund more public transportation options, we need to become a less car-reliant city and embrace 10-minute neighborhoods and more buses and rail and transportation.”
